Thank you, Mr. Chair. First of all, let me express sincere appreciation to you for your leadership. Mr. Chair, the 2019 Ministerial Declaration provides a comprehensive roadmap. And as we look ahead, Thailand believes that a balanced and sustained approach rooted in sustainable development and human security is paramount to achieving our collective goals. Mr. Chair, alternative development remains a cornerstone of the world drug problem solution, linking socioeconomic progress directly to law enforcement success. Thailand is proud of its history as a pioneer in this field, transitioning from a major illicit opium producer to an economy powered by sustainable agriculture and tourism. To ensure this critical approach remains relevant and effective, Thailand, in close partnership with the governments of Peru and Germany, UNODC, and key partners, co-hosted the expert group meeting on alternative development in Lima, Peru, from November 5th to 7th, 2025. This gathering successfully synthesized lessons learned and identified critical gaps in implementing comprehensive, gender-sensitive, and environmentally sound AD programs. The outcome of the Lima EGM provide a vital practitioner-driven complement to the 2013 United Nations Guiding Principles on Alternative Development. Therefore, I am pleased to announce that Thailand, along with Germany and Peru, intend to table a draft resolution on alternative development at the 69th session of the CND in March 2026. This resolution will seek to build upon the existing guiding principles by emphasizing modern challenges and emerging consensus areas, including climate adaptation and resilience as part of climate and environmental sustainability, and the need for greater integration of market access and long-term political commitment to ensure stable programming. We look forward to engaging with all member states to ensure this draft resolution receives broad support and strengthens the global framework for decades to come. Mr. Chair, turning to implementation of the 2019 commitments on supply reduction and cross-border cooperation, the situation in the Golden Triangle demands our immediate and sustained attention. Thailand is escalating its national operation, focusing heavily on disrupting the illicit supply chain at its most vulnerable points. In line with this priority, Thailand prioritizes the control of chemical substances, precursors, the disruption of drug production sources in the Golden Triangle, and uplift the people to tangibly resolve the problem. To achieve these goals, the Narcotics Control Board of Thailand has issued new operational orders, including the establishment of dedicated command units for interdiction and suppression, tasked with a multifaceted approach, emphasizing international cooperation. Mr. Chair, Thailand's evolving policy signals a rebalancing, moving beyond a primary focus on arrests towards a preventive and community-based model. It places emphasis on rehabilitating people who use drugs and creating opportunities for social reintegration, ensuring that individuals who have completed their sentences can contribute positively to their communities. To conclude, Thailand remains resolutely committed to confronting the world drug problem through an integrated approach that leverages both international cooperation and decisive national action against organized crime and precursor trafficking. With regard to human rights implications in drug policy, OSCHR remains deeply concerned by the continued application of the death penalty for drug-related offences. In 2024, 615 people were confirmed to have been executed for drug-related offenses, amounting 40% of global total execution. Unfortunately, this trend continues in 2025. OSCE to recall that, according to the international human rights jurisprudence and standard, the term most serious crimes must be respected applies only to crimes extreme gravity involving international killing. In this context, the OSCE Chair also would like to refer to the recommendation in the International Narcotics Control Board annual reports, which encourages all States that retain the death penalty for drug-related offences to consider abolishing it and commuting death sentences already handed down. OSHR urges all States that maintain the death penalty to establish a moratorium with a view to its complete abolition and, at a minimum, restrict its application to only the most serious crimes, which can never include drug offences as defined under international law. The right to life is a supreme right from which no derogation is permitted, even in situations of armed conflict and other public emergencies that threaten the life of the nation. States should take all measures necessary to prevent extrajudicial killing of people in all circumstances, including in the context of countering the drug problem and whatever the criminal conduct alleged against them. Under international human rights law, the intentional use of lethal force is only permissible as a last resort against individuals who pose an imminent threat to life.
